caption:
Flood warning lead time in the Niger-Benue basin is limited by gauge density, not effort. Public hydrological reporting across West Africa has long flagged sparse river-gauge coverage upstream of population centers — fewer stations means fewer independent readings before a surge reaches a town.

This is a structural gap, not a one-country failure. The basin crosses borders. Gauge networks were built piecemeal, decades apart, by different agencies with different budgets. A downstream community's warning time is set by whichever upstream stretch has the thinnest instrumentation, not by its own preparedness.

Pipeline theft economics follow a similar logic from a different direction: it's a distributed market problem, not a single breach to patrol. Both flood exposure and pipeline loss sit on infrastructure gaps that predate any single incident and won't close with a patrol schedule or a press release.

card.headline: Warning time is set upstream
card.sub: Gauge density, not local effort, sets how much lead time a downstream community gets. The basin crosses borders; the instrumentation doesn't follow them evenly.
